toc.title: Can you build distress tolerance through exposure?
What that looks like in therapy

blocks.p: Two questions come up a lot when I teach Polyvagal 101. How does fawning fit into the Polyvagal Theory? And can you build distress tolerance through repeated, voluntary exposure?

Fawning seems to be something people struggle with a lot. My concern about us polyvagal teachers is that we take the information and try to put our own spin on it, or we bring in other pieces of the trauma-informed realm and throw them all together in a mashup of trauma-informed, or quasi trauma-informed, information. I think fawn is one of those things. People really try to make it fit into the polyvagal states, but I don't think it works quite that way.

Let's bring it back to where we started. The Polyvagal Theory is about biology. It's primarily about biological states, which then come with behaviors and thoughts and feelings and sensations. But the biological autonomic state is the focus.

Fawning doesn't have that. Fawning is not a biological state. I would say fawning is a behavior. I'd call it a behavioral adaptation to a biological state. It may be a behavioral adaptation in order to get needs met, and those needs come from a defensive state. So I'd say that person is probably in flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze.

I'd argue that shutdown has a lot to do with it: a disconnection from the self, from one's sense of self or identity or needs, and sacrificing that in order to appease someone else, and then maybe get basic needs met. I'd argue that shutdown is in there, but I think fawning could come from any of the defensive states.
So fawning is not a state. It's a behavior, or a set of behaviors, that could come from different states. That's how I view it. There is no fawn biology.

With the Polyvagal Theory, we're talking about biology. People in the trauma realm will talk about flight, fight, fawn, freeze, friendship, flop, all kinds of words that start with F. They describe behaviors, which is useful, but those behaviors aren't necessarily directly connected to a biological state.
So as you go out into the internet wilds and hear about trauma stuff, keep that in mind. Is this a behavior, or are they talking about biology?

blocks.h: Can you build distress tolerance through exposure?

blocks.p: There's a video I use when I teach about shutdown. A dad and his daughter are on a rollercoaster. He passes out. The little girl is totally fine. She smiles the whole time, and she has empathy for him. So can somebody gain distress tolerance through repeated, voluntary exposure?

It obviously depends on the person, their life circumstances, all that stuff. But here's what it could look like. Let's say the dad does the ride, passes out, and comes back. They get off the ride. Now they're in literal safety. Their feet are on the ground. They can look at people, make eye contact, smile, maybe laugh it off. And then maybe eventually they say, "Okay, let's try it again." They go back, and the same thing may happen, but maybe it's not as intense.

That's called a neural exercise. We're working out these pathways, just like you'd work out muscles. If you want to lift heavier things, you've got to start off by lifting kind of heavy things. You can't lift 100 pounds unless you lift 50, and you can't lift 50 unless you lift 25. You can build these pathways, specifically the safe and social state. You can build its strength so you're able to tolerate more, to gain distress tolerance.
Dr. Porges put it this way when he was on the podcast:

q: What I wanna proliferate in thinking is the concept of neural exercise... And it's not a question of muscle tone, it's a question of neural flexibility and adaptation.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [Dr Stephen Porges: Polyvagal Theory Updates & Critiques (2023) (episode 201)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/0e6ffc9f-a364-46e7-bb44-a17299f16de6)

blocks.p: But you have to be able to balance it out. You have to be able to go from flight and fight, let's say, to safety, and then back and forth. That's why play is so unbelievably important, especially in childhood, while these pathways are developing: experiencing these states mindfully, and building the strength of these pathways.

blocks.h: What that looks like in therapy

blocks.p: Therapeutically, this would be like exposure therapy. Even just talking about the thing you went through is considered exposure, because you're feeling it again and thinking about it. All that stuff comes up.

ol: You voluntarily say, "Okay, I want to try this out and see how it goes."
You process it, and notice it.
If it becomes too difficult, you stop there. You balance it out with your safety state, and then come back to it.

blocks.p: We want to do a little bit at a time and build a tolerance, so that the next week you come in for therapy, you're way more able to tolerate that same thing, and now you can maybe go a bit deeper into it. That's how we build the strength of your safety state, to be able to handle the distress of whatever it is.

That's a heck of a lot different than coming into therapy and the therapist kicks back and says, "Okay, tell me about your childhood. Now tell me more. And tell me more." They push and push and push, and that's just going to result in dysregulation. That doesn't really help. It may actually be re-traumatizing and reinforcing, and maybe scare that person off from going to therapy altogether.
